title: Company profile (standard text)
text:
Northlight Data Advisory (sample bidder) is an independent digital and data consultancy founded in 2018 in Amsterdam, with a second office in Nairobi opened in 2021. We have 34 staff: 22 consultants, 6 data and information management specialists, and 6 in project support, finance and administration.

We help governments, UN agencies, development banks and NGOs make better decisions with data, and use data and digital tools safely. Our work falls into three practices:
1. Data governance and data protection: national and sector data governance frameworks, data protection impact assessments, data sharing agreements, and responsible AI reviews.
2. Information management: monitoring systems, survey design, dashboards and information management for humanitarian and health programmes.
3. Digital health policy: regulatory mapping, digital health strategies, and interoperability and standards advice.

Since 2018 we have completed 61 assignments in 19 countries, 38 of them for UN agencies or national governments. Working languages are English and French. We do not have Indonesian-speaking staff and partner with national organisations where a tender needs local language and context.

How we work: small senior teams, a named team leader who stays for the whole assignment, two-step quality review on every deliverable, and handover of all working files and templates to the client at the end.

title: Method: stakeholder consultation and focus group discussions
text:
Purpose: to collect, test and validate evidence with the people who will have to apply a policy.

Steps:
1. Stakeholder mapping: list every institution and group affected, score each on influence and interest, and agree the list with the client in the inception phase.
2. Invitations 10 working days ahead, through the client, with a 1 to 2 page pre-read sent 5 working days ahead.
3. Each focus group discussion (FGD) has a facilitator, a note-taker and a client focal point. Hybrid meetings have a second facilitator who manages online participants and the chat.
4. A structured note template captures positions, evidence offered, disagreements and follow-up questions, so notes from different meetings can be compared.
5. Key informant interviews (45 to 60 minutes) fill gaps where a group setting will not work, for example with industry or senior officials.
6. Validation: participants receive a 2-page summary of findings and have 5 working days to comment before findings are final.

Inclusion: we check the participant list for balance across institutions, levels of government, sexes and regions, and report the actual mix in each report.
Typical scale: 15 to 25 participants per FGD; 2 resource persons per meeting.

title: Method: international benchmarking
text:
Purpose: to learn from countries that have already solved a similar problem, and judge what will work in the client's context.

Steps:
1. Agree the benchmarking questions with the client in the inception report. Typical questions: who regulates, how risk is classified, how products are validated before use, and how they are monitored after deployment.
2. Choose 3 to 5 countries using four criteria: relevance of the health system, maturity of the regulation, availability of documents in English, and at least one country with a similar income level.
3. Desk review of laws, regulations, guidance and evaluations, plus 1 or 2 interviews per country with regulators or experts.
4. Compare in a single matrix, one row per question, one column per country.
5. Fit assessment: score each practice on legal fit, institutional capacity, cost and time to implement in the client country.
6. Report the practices worth adopting, adapting or avoiding, with reasons.

International frameworks we use as the reference point: the WHO guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health, the OECD AI Principles, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, and the EU AI Act.

title: Method: policy options analysis and recommendations
text:
We turn findings into decisions a ministry can take.

1. Problem statements: one per priority gap, agreed with the client.
2. Options: for each problem, 2 to 4 options, always including "no new regulation, use existing powers".
3. Assessment criteria: effectiveness, legal feasibility, institutional capacity, cost, time to implement, and risks to patients and to innovation.
4. Scoring with the client's technical team in a working session, then a validation meeting with stakeholders.
5. Recommendations: each one names the responsible institution, the legal instrument (law, regulation, ministerial decree, technical guideline), the first follow-up action and a time frame.
6. A policy brief of 2 to 4 pages for senior decision makers, in plain language.

title: Method: AI governance framework for health
text:
Our framework follows the AI lifecycle, from idea to retirement, and sets minimum requirements for each stage:

1. Scope and risk classification: which AI tools are covered, and a risk tier based on the clinical or administrative impact of an error.
2. Data governance: lawful basis, data quality and representativeness, consent, access control, retention, and links to the national personal data protection law.
3. Model accountability: a named accountable owner for every AI tool, a model registry, documentation (intended use, training data, known limitations), and a route for complaints.
4. Validation and clinical safety: performance thresholds before use, local validation on national data, and clinical safety review for high-risk tools.
5. Monitoring and auditing: post-deployment monitoring of accuracy and bias, incident reporting, periodic algorithm audits by an independent party, and criteria for suspending a tool.
6. Institutions: who regulates, who certifies, who audits, and how the health ministry, data protection authority and medical device regulator work together.

We map each element to the WHO guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health, the OECD AI Principles and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, and then to national law.

title: Quality assurance and risk management
text:
Quality assurance:
- Every deliverable passes a two-step review before it reaches the client: a technical peer review by a senior expert not on the project (2 working days), then an editorial and formatting review (1 working day).
- The team leader signs off each deliverable against the terms of reference using a checklist that lists every required element.
- We track client comments in a comment log, showing how each comment was handled. The log is sent with each revised version.
- Our ISO 9001 quality management system covers project start-up, document control and client feedback.

Risk management:
- A risk register is created in the inception phase and reviewed every two weeks with the client focal point. Each risk has an owner, likelihood, impact and mitigation.
- Typical top risks in a short policy study, with our usual mitigation:
  1. Stakeholders unavailable during consultations: book all meetings in the inception phase, through the client; offer online participation.
  2. Late access to data or documents: list required documents at kick-off; agree a fallback of public sources.
  3. Late review comments from the client: agree review periods in the inception report (usually 5 working days); escalate after 2 days late.
  4. Scope creep: record changes in the risk register and agree them in writing.
  5. Political sensitivity of recommendations: test wording with the client focal point before wider circulation.

Documentation: all working files, notes and templates are stored in a shared client folder and handed over at the end of the assignment.

title: Data protection and confidentiality
text:
- We process personal data only as needed for the assignment, under a data processing agreement where the client is the controller.
- Interview and FGD notes are pseudonymised; participant lists are kept separate from notes, with access limited to the core team.
- Data is stored in the EU (Microsoft 365, EU data boundary), with multi-factor authentication for all staff.
- Personal data is deleted or returned 90 days after the end of the contract, unless the client asks otherwise in writing.
- All staff and associates sign confidentiality undertakings and complete annual data protection training.
- We do not enter client documents into public AI tools. Where AI tools are used to support analysis, they run under enterprise terms with no training on client data, and a person checks every output.

title: Organisation profile: Stichting Buurtklimaat (sample applicant)
text:
Stichting Buurtklimaat Utrecht (sample applicant) helps residents make their own streets cooler, greener and better at holding rainwater. We were founded in 2019 by residents of Utrecht Zuilen after a summer of heat and flooded basements.

We work in neighbourhoods with little green space and many residents on low incomes: Zuilen, Overvecht and Kanaleneiland. We combine three things: physical change in the street (removing paving, rain gardens, green roofs), residents who design, build and maintain it, and partnerships with the municipality and housing corporations who own most of the land.

Team: 6 staff (4.2 FTE): a director, a project lead, two community organisers, a landscape gardener and a part-time finance and office manager. 120 active volunteers, of whom 35 are trained "street captains" who coordinate maintenance in their own street.
Working languages with residents: Dutch, Arabic, Turkish and English.

Results: 16 rain gardens built, about 48,000 litres of storage. 140 residents involved. The housing corporation adopted our rain garden design for two other estates.
Lesson learned: maintenance agreements must be signed before building starts; in two blocks it took 4 months after completion.

title: Theory of change (organisation level)
text:
Problem: in dense, paved neighbourhoods residents suffer most from heat and flooding, and have the least say over their street.
If residents design, build and maintain green measures in their own street, together with the land owners,
then streets become measurably cooler and hold more rainwater,
and residents gain the skills, network and ownership to keep the green alive and to ask for more,
so that the neighbourhood becomes more resilient to climate extremes, and social cohesion grows.
Key assumptions: land owners give permission and commit to maintenance agreements; enough residents take part, including older residents and families; plants survive the first dry summer with watering by street captains.

title: Resident involvement method
text:
1. Street walk with residents to map hot spots and flooding, in the evening and on Saturdays so working residents can join.
2. Kitchen-table design sessions in each street, in Dutch, Arabic, Turkish and English, with drawings rather than plans.
3. Build days where residents and volunteers do the planting together with our gardener.
4. Street captains: one or two residents per street trained to coordinate watering and maintenance, with a small tool kit.
5. Door-to-door visits to reach residents who do not come to meetings, especially older residents living alone.
We record participation by street, age group and activity.

title: Monitoring, evaluation and learning approach
text:
Physical effects: m2 of paving removed (measured on plan and checked on site), number and storage volume of rain gardens (design value), surface temperature on depaved and paved spots with a thermal camera on 3 hot afternoons a year, and air temperature with 10 low-cost sensors per neighbourhood.
Residents: participation by activity and age group, a short survey on heat experience and ownership at start and end (target response 150).
Plants: survival and maintenance check every 6 months.
Learning: a learning session with partners at mid-term and a short public learning note at the end.
Typical cost: 7 to 9% of direct costs.

title: Safeguarding and volunteer policy
text: All staff and street captains who work with residents sign our code of conduct. Staff and volunteers who work with children or vulnerable adults have a certificate of conduct (VOG). We have a confidential adviser and a complaints procedure published on our website. Volunteers are insured through the municipal volunteer insurance. Build days follow our safety checklist, including tool instructions and first aid.
